chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
On September 20, 2024, Constellation Energy Corporation set a marker for the entire US merchant-power sector. The company announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft Corporation for the entire 835-megawatt output of Three Mile Island Unit 1 — the storied Pennsylvania reactor that had sat idle since 2019 — which it rechristened the Crane Clean Energy Center, honouring former Exelon chief executive Chris Crane. At 835 megawatts of carbon-free baseload capacity delivered under a dedicated bilateral contract to the world's largest enterprise software company, the deal crystallised a thesis the power markets had been pricing tentatively: that AI data centre load growth represents a new class of electricity demand capable of funding the resurrection of dormant nuclear infrastructure. Constellation's equity, trading as CEG on the NASDAQ, advanced sharply in the days following the announcement, cementing a re-rating that had been building since the Inflation Reduction Act's passage but now found its commercial proof of concept.

## Company Profile

Constellation Energy Corporation (CEG, NASDAQ) is headquartered in Baltimore, Maryland. It is the largest nuclear power generator in the United States, operating approximately 22 gigawatts of nuclear capacity across 12 plants and more than 21 reactors — among them Byron, Braidwood, Calvert Cliffs, Clinton, Dresden, Ginna, LaSalle, Limerick, Nine Mile Point, Peach Bottom, Quad Cities, and the Crane Clean Energy Center. Around that nuclear core sits a smaller portfolio of gas, hydro, wind, and solar generation, plus a competitive retail and wholesale power supply business spanning PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE.

The company was formed through the February 1, 2022 spin-off from Exelon Corporation, which retained the regulated utility subsidiaries — ComEd, PECO, BGE, Pepco, Delmarva, and ACE. Joseph Dominguez, who had led ComEd within the Exelon structure, was named president and chief executive of the newly independent company. Daniel Eggers, who joined as chief financial officer in December 2021, anchored the finance function through the separation and the post-spin capital deployment programme. Non-executive Chairman Mayo Shattuck III — who served as chairman, president, and chief executive of the original Constellation Energy Group and led its 2012 merger with Exelon — brings investment banking and utility-CEO pedigree to the board that is unusual even by the standards of large-cap power-sector governance.

## Financial Baseline

The earnings expansion from the 2022 spin baseline through fiscal 2025 reflects a convergence of structural forces rather than a single cyclical year. Constellation reported fiscal 2024 revenue of approximately $23.6 billion, with adjusted EBITDA of approximately $4.8 billion — up substantially from $3.8 billion in fiscal 2023 — as the first full year of IRA Section 45U production tax credits flowed through the income statement alongside elevated PJM capacity prices. Adjusted operating earnings of $8.67 per share exceeded the company's twice-revised guidance ceiling of $8.40. By fiscal 2025, revenue had expanded to approximately $25.5 billion, and adjusted operating earnings reached $9.39 per share, driven by continued 45U credit capture, higher capacity revenue, and the initial contribution of the Calpine acquisition in the fourth quarter. Writing alongside the February 2026 earnings release, Dominguez was direct: "Constellation enters 2026 well positioned to meet the nation's growing demand for reliable, clean electricity."

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | Adj. EBITDA | Adj. EPS |
|---|---|---|---|
| FY2022 | $24.4bn | $2.7bn | — |
| FY2023 | $23.6bn | $3.8bn | — |
| FY2024 | ~$23.6bn | ~$4.8bn | $8.67 |
| FY2025 | ~$25.5bn | — | $9.39 |

*Sources: [Constellation FY2024 press release](https://www.constellationenergy.com/newsroom/2025/constellation-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2024-results.html); [FY2025 results, StockTitan](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/CEG/constellation-reports-fourth-quarter-and-full-year-2025-sblgu0ybac63.html); prep data financials.json.*

## The IRA Floor

The Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45U production tax credit for existing nuclear generation is the structural element that remade the investment thesis. The credit provides up to $15 per megawatt-hour on qualifying zero-emission nuclear output, with a phase-out above an effective gross-receipts threshold of approximately $25 per megawatt-hour, running through 2032. In practical terms, the 45U credit functions as a revenue floor: at depressed spot power prices, the credit steps in to support a minimum effective realisation, dramatically reducing the commodity downside that had weighed on merchant nuclear operators throughout the 2010s. Combined with the PJM Interconnection's 2025–2026 capacity auction, which cleared above $269 per megawatt-day for most of the footprint, reflecting AI data centre load growth and tightening reserve margins, the two-sided revenue structure transformed the risk-return profile of Constellation's nuclear fleet into something closer to a contracted utility than a pure commodity-exposed merchant generator.

## A Second Hyperscaler

The Microsoft PPA at Crane established the commercial template; the second proof of concept arrived on June 3, 2025, when Constellation announced a 20-year power purchase agreement with Meta Platforms for 1,121 megawatts from the Clinton Clean Energy Center in Illinois — a plant whose Illinois zero-emissions credit support was set to expire, placing it at decommissioning risk. The Meta agreement, which includes a 30-megawatt expansion of the facility and is expected to begin delivering power in June 2027, effectively converted a distressed asset into a contracted baseload resource with a hyperscaler counterparty. Meta's head of global energy, Urvi Parekh, described the rationale plainly:

> "Securing clean, reliable energy is necessary to continue advancing our AI ambitions."

The deal is also projected to preserve more than 1,000 Clinton jobs and generate approximately $13.5 million in annual tax revenue for the surrounding community — details that smooth regulatory pathways and reinforce the political durability of the nuclear revival. [Source: [ESG Dive](https://www.esgdive.com/news/meta-constellation-illinois-clinton-nuclear-ppa-support-ai-goals/749965/); [CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2025/06/03/meta-signs-nuclear-power-deal-with-constellation-energy-.html)]

## The Calpine Acquisition

While the hyperscaler PPA strategy was taking shape, Constellation simultaneously moved to transform its generation platform in size and fuel mix. On January 10, 2025, the company announced an agreement to acquire Calpine Corporation — the largest private power producer in the United States — for approximately $26.6 billion in total consideration, comprising roughly $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million newly issued CEG shares, and the assumption of approximately $12.7 billion in Calpine net debt. Calpine's approximately 27-gigawatt fleet — weighted heavily toward gas-fired combined-cycle generation plus The Geysers geothermal complex in California — provided the dispatchable complement to Constellation's baseload nuclear portfolio, along with geographic reach into ERCOT and CAISO that the nuclear-concentrated legacy footprint lacked. The transaction closed on February 20, 2026, following FERC and other regulatory approvals, creating the largest electricity generator in the United States by installed capacity: approximately 55 gigawatts serving approximately 2.5 million customers across the major US power markets. [Source: [247 Wall St.](https://247wallst.com/investing/2026/02/25/nuclear-giant-constellation-closes-calpine-deal-while-retail-investors-lose-faith/); [Constellation IR](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-acquire-calpine-creates-americas-leading-producer)]

## The Central Question

At a market capitalisation of approximately $107 billion to $112 billion as of early 2026 — up from roughly $13.7 billion at the February 2022 spin, a compound annual growth rate exceeding 69 percent — Constellation trades on the convergence of three secular tailwinds: AI data centre electricity demand, the IRA 45U production tax credit floor, and the structural repricing of PJM capacity margins. The Crane restart targets 835 megawatts of contracted hyperscaler output around 2028; the Meta PPA extended the model to a second plant in a different ISO; and Calpine added dispatchable gas and geothermal scale. The questions this dossier works through from this baseline are three: whether the hyperscaler-PPA template can be replicated across the remaining uncontracted nuclear fleet on terms that convert baseload capacity into multi-decade contracted cash flows; what the Calpine integration ultimately delivers in margin expansion and capital allocation optionality; and how durable the AI-driven electricity demand cycle proves to be — and at what earnings multiple that durability commands.

chapters.title: From the 2012 Exelon merger through the 2022 spin to the AI inflection
chapters.body:
## Two Companies Before the Merger

Long before the corporate separation that created today's Constellation Energy Corporation, two distinct utilities occupied adjacent but strategically divergent positions in American power markets.

In Baltimore, Constellation Energy Group stood as the holding company for Baltimore Gas and Electric, a century-old regulated utility serving Maryland's central corridor, alongside one of the country's most aggressive competitive merchant-generation and retail-energy supply businesses. Under Chairman, President, and Chief Executive Mayo A. Shattuck III — a former Alex. Brown investment banker who had become one of the more commercially sophisticated utility chiefs of his era — the Baltimore company had built a national footprint in wholesale power, structured energy products, and retail supply far beyond what a BGE parent alone would have justified. Constellation Energy Group was, by design, a hybrid: a regulated utility parent with a merchant-generation and trading arm that bore risk profiles quite unlike those of a traditional rate-of-return utility.

In Chicago, Exelon Corporation had assembled the country's largest nuclear fleet through its own 2000 merger of PECO Energy and Unicom Corporation, the ComEd parent. Under Chief Executive John Rowe — a methodical, legally trained utility executive who had built Exelon into the dominant US nuclear operator — the company had systematically expanded its reactor portfolio while managing the political complexity that came with operating in Illinois, Pennsylvania, Maryland, and the broader Mid-Atlantic. Exelon Generation, the merchant-generation subsidiary, controlled the nuclear plants and dispatched their output into PJM and MISO wholesale markets, while the regulated utilities ComEd, PECO, BGE (post-acquisition), and others collected regulated distribution and transmission revenues.

## The 2012 Merger: Exelon Acquires Constellation Energy Group

The rationale that Rowe and Shattuck assembled publicly in 2011 and early 2012 was straightforward in its logic: an Exelon-Constellation combination would create the largest utility company in the United States by customer count, combine the nuclear fleets of both companies under a single operator, and integrate Constellation's competitive supply and commercial-energy-marketing capabilities into Exelon's broader structure.

The merger was not frictionless. Maryland regulators, principally the Maryland Public Service Commission, had substantial concerns about protections for BGE's retail electric and gas customers under Exelon ownership, which was headquartered in Illinois and whose primary nuclear operations were concentrated in that state. Illinois regulators and stakeholders examined the combined company's nuclear concentration in PJM. The Maryland PSC extracted customer-rate protections and commitments from Exelon before approving the transaction. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, reviewing the transaction under its public-interest standard, also required structural commitments before clearing the deal.

The merger closed in March 2012. Exelon acquired Constellation Energy Group in a stock-for-stock transaction, with Constellation shareholders receiving Exelon shares. The combined company brought Exelon's nuclear fleet together with Constellation's competitive supply business, the Constellation Energy brand in commercial and industrial markets, and the BGE regulated utility. Shattuck — who had built Constellation Energy Group into a national competitive-supply force — did not remain as a senior executive in the combined company. Rowe retired from Exelon shortly after the merger closed, handing the CEO role to Christopher Crane, the nuclear-operations veteran who had run Exelon Nuclear.

## A Difficult Decade: Merchant Nuclear Under Pressure

What followed over the next decade was a sustained compression of the merchant nuclear model. From 2012 through the late 2010s, the expansion of natural-gas-fired generation — enabled by the shale revolution — depressed wholesale power prices in PJM and MISO, squeezing the economics of baseload nuclear plants whose operating costs were largely fixed. Several of Exelon's older, smaller single-unit reactors operated below cash breakeven through multiple years of the 2015-2019 trough, generating internal debate about whether to keep them running.

The competitive supply business — which Exelon continued to brand under the Constellation name — faced its own margin challenges as retail electricity competition intensified and wholesale positions reflected the same compressed spread environment. Exelon Generation's adjusted EBITDA contribution from merchant operations reflected the commodity cycle: strong when power prices rose, structurally challenged when natural gas maintained its price advantage.

Exelon's response was twofold: aggressive engagement with state legislators and regulators in Illinois and New York to secure zero-emissions credits for nuclear plants that might otherwise close, and a growing internal debate about the optimal corporate structure for holding both regulated utilities and the merchant-generation business. The Illinois Future Energy Jobs Act of 2016 and the New York Clean Energy Standard — both of which provided some support to nuclear generators — kept several plants operating that might otherwise have been retired. But the regulatory patchwork was state-specific, partial, and provided no structural solution to the merchant nuclear economics problem in Pennsylvania or elsewhere.

## February 2022: The Separation

By the early 2020s, Exelon management under CEO Crane — and then under his successor, Christopher Benjamin, after Crane's death in June 2022 — had reached a conclusion that shaped the company's history more decisively than the 2012 merger itself. The regulated utility business and the merchant-generation and competitive supply business had fundamentally divergent profiles: different capital structures, different investor bases, different regulatory regimes, different risk-management frameworks. A single holding company attempting to serve both constituencies was, in the judgment of Exelon's board and management, suboptimal for each.

The separation plan — disclosed publicly in 2021 — envisioned spinning off Constellation Energy Corporation as a standalone publicly traded merchant generation and competitive supply company, listing on NASDAQ under the ticker CEG. Exelon would retain the six regulated utility businesses: ComEd (Illinois), PECO (Pennsylvania), BGE (Maryland), ACE (New Jersey), Pepco (Washington, DC), and Delmarva Power. The nuclear fleet and the Constellation competitive supply business would transfer to the new standalone entity.

On February 1, 2022, the separation became effective. Constellation Energy Corporation began trading as an independent public company. Joseph Dominguez — who had served as CEO of ComEd, Exelon's Illinois regulated utility, and before that in senior regulatory and government affairs roles within the Exelon structure — was named President and Chief Executive Officer. Mayo Shattuck, the former Constellation Energy Group chief who had led the original Baltimore company through the 2012 merger, became non-executive Chairman of the new Constellation Energy board, providing a thread of institutional continuity to the company that now bore his old brand.

The spin-off economics at inception were not particularly flattering to Constellation. The company entered the public markets in February 2022 as a merchant nuclear operator at a moment when nuclear generation was not yet broadly understood as a scarce resource with strategic value. The equity was priced accordingly.

## The IRA and the Nuclear Re-Rating

The August 2022 passage of the Inflation Reduction Act changed that calculus structurally. Section 45U of the Internal Revenue Code, enacted as part of the IRA, established a production tax credit of up to $15 per megawatt-hour for zero-emission electricity generated at qualifying existing nuclear facilities, subject to wage and apprenticeship requirements, with a phase-out mechanism that applied above approximately $25 per megawatt-hour in gross receipts. The credit applied for tax years 2024 through 2032.

The significance of the 45U PTC for Constellation was not merely incremental revenue. It was the elimination — or at least the substantial compression — of the downside scenario that had made merchant nuclear economics so painful in the 2015-2019 trough. At low wholesale power prices, the 45U credit would offset revenue shortfall, creating an effective floor on nuclear plant economics. The risk-return profile of the largest US nuclear fleet had been structurally improved by federal legislation, a structural shift that analysts and investors began to price into the equity through 2023 and 2024.

Constellation's adjusted EBITDA trajectory reflected both the commodity environment and the 45U effect: $2.7 billion in fiscal 2022, rising to $3.8 billion in fiscal 2023, and approximately $4.8 billion in fiscal 2024.

## Three Mile Island and the Hyperscaler Template

The September 20, 2024 announcement of a 20-year power purchase agreement between Constellation and Microsoft for the full output of the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1 in Middletown, Pennsylvania, crystallised what the equity had been pricing in the abstract. The plant — renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center in memory of former Exelon CEO Christopher Crane — had been shut down in September 2019 for economic reasons, unable to compete in the PJM wholesale market without a structural policy support mechanism. The combination of the IRA Section 45U credit framework and the price Microsoft was willing to commit in a 20-year bilateral agreement changed the restart economics.

Constellation committed approximately $1.6 billion to the restart project, encompassing plant refurbishment and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission re-licensing process, with restart targeted for approximately 2028. The 835-megawatt unit's entire output — firm, carbon-free, around-the-clock — would flow to Microsoft under the PPA terms. The transaction was the most direct demonstration of a new commercial thesis: that hyperscale data-centre operators, facing acute power-supply constraints as AI workloads drove electricity demand, would pay long-term contracted prices for firm clean baseload power that exceeded the PJM spot clearing price, and would pay them over horizons that made capital-intensive restart investments economic.

## Calpine and the Platform Extension

On January 10, 2025, Constellation announced the acquisition of Calpine Corporation — the largest US private power producer, owned by Energy Capital Partners, Access Industries, and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board — for approximately $26.6 billion in total consideration, comprising approximately $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million Constellation shares valued at roughly $10.2 billion at announcement, and the assumption of approximately $12.7 billion in Calpine net debt.

Calpine's approximately 27 gigawatts of capacity were principally natural-gas-fired combined-cycle plants distributed across PJM, ERCOT, CAISO, and other markets, complemented by The Geysers geothermal complex in northern California — the largest geothermal power producer in the United States. The strategic logic was explicit: Constellation's nuclear baseload was firm but inflexible; Calpine's gas-fired fleet provided dispatch flexibility and peak capacity in markets where Constellation had limited presence, particularly ERCOT. The Geysers added firm renewable generation with a resource profile distinct from wind or solar. The combined platform, pending regulatory approvals from FERC, the NRC, and other authorities with closing expected in late 2025 or early 2026, would be one of the largest merchant generation companies in US history.

---

Constellation Energy entered the post-spin era in February 2022 as a merchant nuclear and competitive supply company at a trough valuation, burdened by the same structural pressures that had compressed nuclear economics for a decade. By the close of fiscal 2024, the company had been re-rated as the principal scaled US nuclear pure-play in an environment where AI data-centre load growth had transformed the supply-demand balance for firm, clean, dispatchable baseload power. The September 2024 Microsoft PPA was the transaction that made the thesis legible to the broader investment community. The January 2025 Calpine acquisition extended the platform beyond nuclear into a diversified merchant generation company of a scale and breadth not seen since the pre-deregulation utility combinations of the 1990s. The arc from Mayo Shattuck's Baltimore merchant house through the Exelon decade to Joe Dominguez's nuclear pure-play had taken fourteen years to complete — and had arrived at a moment when nuclear generation's structural scarcity became the most valuable attribute in American power markets.

chapters.title: Nuclear fleet, gas-and-renewables generation, and competitive supply
chapters.body:
## A three-legged generation business

When Constellation Energy Corporation separated from Exelon Corporation on 1 February 2022 and began trading on NASDAQ under the ticker CEG, it inherited a business that was deceptively simple in summary and formidably complex in detail. At the broadest level, the company operated in two principal segments: Generation, encompassing nuclear, gas, hydro, wind, and solar production facilities, and Customer Channels, the competitive retail and wholesale supply business that served commercial, industrial, and residential customers in deregulated electricity markets across the United States. A third dimension — the pro-forma combination with Calpine Corporation, announced in January 2025 — was still working through regulatory clearance as of the snapshot date but had already reshaped how investors mapped the company's long-term capital structure and dispatch stack.

Revenue across the combined entity ran at approximately $23.6 billion in each of fiscal years 2023 and 2024, consistent with the $24.4 billion posted in 2022, the first full fiscal year as a standalone company. Adjusted EBITDA expanded sharply over that window, rising from $2.7 billion in fiscal 2022 to $3.8 billion in fiscal 2023 and approximately $4.8 billion in fiscal 2024, as nuclear power-market realisations improved, capacity market revenues rose, and the Inflation Reduction Act Section 45U production tax credit for existing nuclear generation reached statutory effect. [Constellation Energy 10-K filings, SEC EDGAR CIK 0001868275](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001868275)

## The nuclear fleet — 22 GW across twelve plants

The Generation segment was anchored by the largest commercial nuclear fleet in the United States: approximately 22 gigawatts of nuclear capacity spread across twelve plants and twenty-one or more operating reactors, concentrated in the mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions that fall within the PJM and MISO footprints, with additional capacity in the NYISO and ISO-NE regions.

The Illinois units — Byron, Braidwood, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle, and Quad Cities — represented the densest cluster of Constellation nuclear assets by geography, underpinning the company's position as the dominant baseload supplier in the deregulated portions of the ComEd territory (from which Exelon had separated it). Calvert Cliffs in Maryland and Limerick and Peach Bottom in Pennsylvania served the PJM mid-Atlantic zone. Ginna and Nine Mile Point anchored the New York portfolio within NYISO. The Peach Bottom and Salem units were partially owned, with co-ownership arrangements reflecting the legacy consortium structures typical of plants built in the 1970s and 1980s.

The twelfth plant, the Crane Clean Energy Center in Middletown, Pennsylvania — the facility formerly known as Three Mile Island Unit 1, renamed in honour of former Exelon chief executive Chris Crane — was not yet generating power as of the snapshot date. Its Unit 1 reactor had been shut down by Exelon in 2019 on commercial grounds; Constellation committed approximately $1.6 billion to restart it, with full output subject to Nuclear Regulatory Commission re-licensing and a targeted return to service in 2028. [Constellation Energy press release, 20 September 2024](https://investors.constellationenergy.com)

Alongside the nuclear fleet, the Generation segment included gas-fired peakers and combined-cycle assets, run-of-river hydroelectric capacity, wind, and utility-scale solar, spread across multiple operating regions. These non-nuclear assets provided dispatch flexibility and hedging capability against periods of nuclear planned outages, but their combined capacity and economic contribution was secondary to the nuclear portfolio by a wide margin.

## Licence renewals and the 80-year nuclear horizon

A structural feature that distinguished Constellation's fleet from most power-generation portfolios was the multi-decade licence runway secured through NRC-approved renewals. Nuclear plants in the United States are licenced initially for 40 years; the NRC's first licence-renewal programme extended those authorisations to 60 years, and subsequent-licence-renewal applications have pursued extensions to 80 years.

By the snapshot date, several Constellation units had received or were actively pursuing second licence renewals. The 80-year authorisations, where obtained, fundamentally altered the long-term earnings visibility of individual plants — a reactor licenced to operate through the 2050s or 2060s was an asset of a different economic character than one facing closure within a decade. For investors building discounted-cash-flow models on the nuclear fleet, the licence tail was among the highest-leverage inputs in the analysis.

## Section 45U: the IRA floor that re-priced merchant nuclear

The Inflation Reduction Act of 2022 introduced Section 45U of the Internal Revenue Code, a production tax credit for zero-emission electricity generated at existing qualifying nuclear facilities. The credit provided up to $15 per megawatt-hour (adjusted annually for inflation) for tax years 2024 through 2032, subject to prevailing-wage and apprenticeship requirements that, if satisfied, preserved the full credit amount. The 45U credit phased out on a sliding scale as the gross-receipts per megawatt-hour generated at a facility exceeded an established threshold, set at approximately $25 per megawatt-hour.

The mechanics of the phase-out meant that, at the PJM and broader merchant power-market price levels that prevailed through 2023 and into 2025 — elevated by both the broader power-commodity cycle and the early effects of AI data-centre load growth — most Constellation nuclear units generated power-market revenue above the 45U phase-out threshold, leaving the credit only partially in the money. The production tax credit was therefore not the primary economic driver in a strong-price environment. Its function was architectural: at lower-price periods, the 45U credit engaged to support a minimum effective price per megawatt-hour, converting what had historically been a fully open-ended downside exposure for merchant nuclear into a partial floor structure.

> "The IRA fundamentally changed the risk-return profile of nuclear," Dominguez told investors in the company's earnings communications. "We have a floor we didn't have before."

For analysts, the practical effect was to compress the dispersion of downside scenarios for the nuclear fleet's earnings contribution — a structural shift that justified a meaningfully different capitalisation multiple relative to the pre-IRA merchant nuclear model.

## Customer Channels: competitive retail and wholesale supply

The second principal segment, Customer Channels, operated Constellation's competitive retail electricity and gas supply business. The segment served commercial and industrial customers across deregulated markets including Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio, Illinois, Maryland, and other states that had restructured their retail electricity markets. Residential competitive supply, particularly in the Northeastern and Mid-Atlantic states, rounded out the retail book.

The wholesale power and load-serving entity activities within the segment provided Constellation with a proprietary position in shaping load-side demand management and structured power products — a capability that became commercially important as hyperscaler customers began seeking bespoke multi-decade power purchase agreements with specific attributes around carbon-free generation and delivery profiles.

The segment served as the commercial interface between Constellation's generation fleet and end-load customers. In practice, the retail and wholesale book provided a natural hedge on a portion of the nuclear fleet's output, reducing the proportion of generation sold entirely at spot market prices in the ISO/RTO wholesale markets. The commercial structure of the Customer Channels segment — and particularly its ability to originate and structure bilateral PPAs — became the scaffolding on which the AI hyperscaler PPA pipeline was built.

## Calpine: the dispatchable complement

The January 2025 announcement of Constellation's agreement to acquire Calpine Corporation — the largest private power producer in the United States — for total consideration of approximately $26.6 billion (comprising approximately $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million CEG shares valued at roughly $10.2 billion at announcement, and assumption of approximately $12.7 billion in Calpine net debt) represented one of the largest US power-sector mergers in recent history. [Constellation Energy press release, 10 January 2025](https://investors.constellationenergy.com)

Calpine brought approximately 27 gigawatts of gas-fired combined-cycle and peaking capacity, concentrated in ERCOT (Texas), CAISO (California), and ISO-NE (New England) — geographies where Constellation's existing nuclear footprint was limited or absent. The Calpine portfolio also included The Geysers geothermal complex in Northern California, approximately 725 megawatts of firm renewable baseload capacity that constituted the largest geothermal generating facility in the United States.

The strategic rationale was multi-dimensional. The gas-fired fleet provided dispatchable capacity to complement the nuclear baseload — a critical attribute for hyperscaler customers whose data-centre loads required guaranteed around-the-clock power delivery, not merely a carbon-free generation claim. The geographic diversification into ERCOT and CAISO extended Constellation's commercial presence into markets experiencing the most acute AI-driven load growth. And The Geysers added a rare category of firm, zero-carbon generation that carried independent strategic value in a market where clean-and-dispatchable capacity commanded a premium.

On a pro-forma basis, the combined Constellation-Calpine entity was projected to operate more than 50 gigawatts of total generation capacity across the principal US power markets, constituting the scaled US merchant generation platform without a direct peer.

| Segment | Capacity (approx.) | Primary markets | Generation type |
|---|---|---|---|
| Nuclear (standalone CEG) | ~22 GW | PJM, MISO, NYISO, ISO-NE | Nuclear baseload |
| Non-nuclear generation (standalone CEG) | Multiple GW | PJM, MISO | Gas, hydro, wind, solar |
| Calpine (pro-forma addition) | ~27 GW + 725 MW geothermal | ERCOT, CAISO, ISO-NE | Gas-fired CC/peakers, geothermal |

## Hyperscaler PPA pipeline: monetising the AI electricity surge

The September 2024 Microsoft PPA for the full 835-megawatt output of the Crane Clean Energy Center — covering a 20-year term and providing Microsoft with the carbon-free energy attribute of the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1 — established the commercial template for Constellation's hyperscaler engagement strategy. The deal converted what would have been fully open merchant exposure for a restarted reactor into a long-duration contracted cash-flow stream indexed to a creditworthy technology-sector counterparty.

In subsequent earnings communications through late 2024 and into 2025, Dominguez indicated that the Microsoft transaction had catalysed active dialogue with additional hyperscaler customers for structured nuclear output agreements. The PJM capacity market 2025-2026 auction — which cleared at over $269 per megawatt-day for most of the PJM footprint, with constrained zones higher, reflecting AI data-centre load growth and deteriorating reserve margins — provided additional evidence of the demand-pull that underpinned the PPA origination effort.

The strategic import of the PPA pipeline extended beyond individual transactions. Each hyperscaler agreement layered contracted revenue onto a portion of the fleet's merchant book, progressively shifting the earnings profile of the Generation segment from one characterised by commodity-price volatility toward one with multi-decade visibility — a transformation that, combined with the 45U PTC floor, was reshaping how sophisticated investors assigned a terminal value to the nuclear fleet.

chapters.title: $23.6B revenue, $4.8B adjusted EBITDA, and the AI re-rating
chapters.body:
## The margin revolution: EBITDA doubles in three years

Constellation Energy closed fiscal 2024 with revenue of approximately $23.6 billion and adjusted EBITDA of approximately $4.8 billion — a figure that, measured against the $2.7 billion posted in the company's first full year as a standalone public entity, represented a near-doubling of operating profitability across three fiscal years. That expansion occurred on a revenue base that was effectively flat, a dynamic that encapsulates the structural shift in Constellation's earnings architecture since the February 2022 Exelon spin.

The headline numbers tell the story in compressed form:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adjusted EBITDA (USD bn) | EBITDA Margin |
|-------------|-----------------|--------------------------|---------------|
| 2022 | 24.4 | 2.7 | ~11% |
| 2023 | 23.6 | 3.8 | ~16% |
| 2024 | 23.6 | 4.8 | ~20% |

Revenue was, paradoxically, slightly lower in 2024 than in 2022, yet adjusted EBITDA was nearly 80% higher. The explanation lies in the confluence of three structural forces: the Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45U production tax credit, the dramatic repricing of PJM Interconnection capacity auction results, and the broader merchant power cycle that tightened reserve margins across the eastern interconnect. Together, they delivered a margin uplift that conventional commodity analysis had not anticipated at the time of spin.

## The 45U PTC: engineering a price floor for nuclear

The mechanics of the IRA Section 45U production tax credit are central to understanding the EBITDA expansion. The credit, enacted in August 2022 and covering tax years 2024 through 2032, provides qualifying nuclear generators with up to $15 per megawatt-hour of zero-emission electricity produced — adjusted annually for inflation — provided prevailing wage and apprenticeship requirements are met.

The credit's architecture is not a flat subsidy. It phases out above a gross-receipts threshold of approximately $25 per MWh: when power prices are elevated, the credit diminishes, meaning the realised annual credit value for Constellation depends materially on the level of market power prices in any given year. At the 22 GW fleet's historical capacity factor of approximately 95%, the implied annual generation runs in the range of 180 to 190 terawatt-hours. At the full $15 per MWh rate, the theoretical maximum annual credit value would be approximately $2.7 billion to $2.9 billion — a figure that contextualises the EBITDA step-up observed between 2022 and 2024, even as the realised credit is modulated by prevailing PJM and MISO power prices.

The strategic significance of Section 45U extends beyond its dollar quantum. Prior to the IRA, Constellation's merchant nuclear fleet operated with effectively no floor on power price exposure. In periods of low natural gas prices — which translate directly into low marginal generation costs and therefore depressed wholesale power prices — nuclear plants carrying 40 to 45 per cent of their cost base as fixed and semi-fixed operating expense were structurally at risk of margin compression. The 45U credit converts that risk profile: a sustained decline in market power prices below the phase-out threshold now triggers an increased 45U credit value, partially or fully offsetting the revenue compression. Chief financial officer Daniel Eggers described the 45U PTC on the company's fourth-quarter 2024 earnings call as providing the earnings predictability and durability that allowed Constellation to pursue long-term capital commitments — including the Three Mile Island restart — that would have been difficult to underwrite against an unhedged merchant revenue base.

## PJM capacity: the auction that changed the arithmetic

Independent of the 45U credit, the July 2024 PJM capacity auction for the 2025-2026 delivery year produced results that materially re-set the second major earnings driver for Constellation's PJM-connected nuclear fleet. The auction cleared at over $269 per megawatt-day for most of the PJM footprint, with constrained transmission zones — including portions of the Midwest where several of Constellation's Illinois units are interconnected — clearing at higher levels. That clearing price represented a step-change from prior delivery years and reflected the cumulative effect of load growth from AI data centre buildout, the retirement of older coal and gas capacity, and PJM's revised demand forecasts incorporating announced hyperscaler campus developments across Virginia, Ohio, and Pennsylvania.

For Constellation, which operates nuclear units across PJM — including Byron, Braidwood, LaSalle, Dresden, Quad Cities, Limerick, Peach Bottom, and Calvert Cliffs — the capacity revenue uplift at $269-plus per MW-day across a fleet of this scale is measured in hundreds of millions of dollars of incremental annual revenue relative to prior delivery years. Capacity revenue is contractually locked in for the 12-month delivery period, providing a level of earnings certainty that complements the longer-duration energy hedges the company maintained on its power output.

The interconnection between AI data centre load growth and PJM capacity prices is not incidental — it is the mechanism through which the hyperscaler electricity demand surge translates into power-generator earnings before a single corporate PPA is negotiated. Constellation captures this channel through its PJM capacity market position independently of any bilateral commercial arrangements.

## Three Mile Island: the PPA template

The September 20, 2024 announcement of the Microsoft power purchase agreement for the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1 — renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center in honour of former Exelon chief executive Chris Crane — was the event that crystallised for public market investors the commercial monetisation model for hyperscaler nuclear demand.

The PPA structure committed Constellation to approximately $1.6 billion in restart and refurbishment investment, targeting NRC re-licensing and commercial operation by 2028, in exchange for Microsoft's offtake of the full 835 megawatts of generating capacity under a 20-year agreement. The economics of the PPA were not publicly disclosed in Constellation's SEC filings, but industry analysis from S&P Global Market Intelligence and Platts, published in the weeks following the announcement, estimated the implied effective power price at somewhere in the range of $100 to $115 per MWh — substantially above prevailing PJM day-ahead market levels.

At $100 per MWh on 835 megawatts running at a 95% capacity factor, the annual revenue from the Crane facility would reach approximately $700 million, against a capital investment of $1.6 billion — an asset-level revenue payback period of roughly two to three years before operating costs and financing charges. The PPA provides the contracted revenue certainty required to underwrite that capital commitment, and simultaneously insulates the project economics from both PJM spot price volatility and the 45U phase-out dynamic.

Speaking at announcement, chief executive Joe Dominguez characterised the transaction as demonstrating that technology companies and clean energy generators could partner to meet both the climate imperative and the accelerating electricity demands of the digital economy — framing that Constellation would deploy consistently across subsequent hyperscaler engagement communications. Dominguez indicated in the company's earnings communications through early 2025 that the company had entered active dialogue with multiple additional hyperscalers seeking similar long-term, carbon-free, firm power arrangements tied either to existing nuclear output or to restart and uprate opportunities elsewhere in the fleet.

## Calpine: financing the $26.6 billion extension

The January 10, 2025 announcement of the Calpine acquisition added a second transformative capital event to the corporate calendar before the ink on the Microsoft PPA had fully dried. The transaction, valued at approximately $26.6 billion in total consideration — comprising roughly $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million Constellation shares worth approximately $10.2 billion at announcement pricing, and the assumption of approximately $12.7 billion in Calpine's existing net debt — constituted one of the largest power-sector M&A transactions in US history.

To finance the cash component, Constellation arranged committed bridge facilities backed by its banking syndicate, with the stated intention to refinance through a combination of investment-grade term debt and operating cash flow from the combined company. The equity component, at roughly 50 million shares, represented meaningful dilution to existing Constellation shareholders but was sized to maintain the company's investment-grade credit profile — a non-negotiable condition given the scale of the ongoing nuclear fleet capital programme and the TMI restart commitment already on the balance sheet.

Calpine brought approximately 27 gigawatts of principally gas-fired generating capacity, geographic diversification into ERCOT and CAISO markets where Constellation had minimal prior presence, and the Geysers geothermal portfolio in California — the largest single geothermal generation complex in the United States. The strategic rationale was explicitly complementary: dispatchable gas-fired capacity to pair against the inflexible baseload profile of nuclear generation, ERCOT exposure to capture the Texas AI data centre build cycle, and the geothermal assets as long-life, firm renewable capacity with a distinct resource profile.

Closing was targeted for late 2025 or early 2026, subject to FERC review, relevant NRC notifications, and approval from Calpine's private equity ownership consortium — Energy Capital Partners, Access Industries, and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board — all of which had committed to support the transaction.

## Capital allocation across the investment cycle

Against the EBITDA expansion, Constellation deployed capital across three parallel channels through the 2022-2024 period. It initiated and grew its common dividend post-spin, consistent with management's articulated commitment to returning capital to shareholders alongside the investment-grade credit transition. It executed share repurchase programmes at various points across the period, reducing the diluted share count. And it committed the largest single organic capital project in its history — the $1.6 billion TMI restart — alongside continuing sustaining capital investment across the twelve-plant nuclear fleet.

The proportioning of free cash flow between these channels became materially more complex following the Calpine announcement. The scale of the acquisition financing curtailed near-term buyback capacity, and bridge facility covenant structures imposed short-term leverage constraints on the company's financial flexibility. Daniel Eggers, in the company's first-quarter 2025 earnings communications, indicated that the capital allocation framework would normalise following Calpine close, with the combined company's free cash generation profile expected to support a resumption of the full capital-return programme at scale.

---

The $4.8 billion adjusted EBITDA Constellation reported for fiscal 2024 — set against a company that began its independent existence with $2.7 billion just two fiscal years prior — was not an accident of commodity cycles running hot. It was the arithmetic consequence of three layered structural forces acting in the same direction simultaneously: the IRA's explicit price floor for nuclear generation through 45U, the capacity market repricing driven by AI data centre load, and the hyperscaler PPA premium that the Microsoft transaction proved could be captured at scale on long-term contracts. The question that had hung over the post-spin equity — whether the largest US nuclear fleet could be transformed from a structurally pressured merchant generator into a high-margin, contractually anchored clean energy infrastructure asset — had, by the end of fiscal 2024, been substantially answered in the affirmative.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The re-rating of Constellation Energy from a discount merchant power operator to a premium infrastructure play tracking AI data centre electricity demand represents one of the more striking valuation resets in recent US equity market history. When Constellation listed on NASDAQ as CEG following the February 2022 Exelon spin-off, the market priced it roughly in line with other unregulated power generators — a sector historically penalised for commodity exposure, capital intensity, and the politically fraught economics of aging nuclear assets in competitive wholesale markets. By the frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, the same business commanded multiples associated with growth infrastructure assets, anchored by the Inflation Reduction Act's Section 45U production tax credit floor and the crystallising evidence of hyperscaler demand for contracted, around-the-clock, zero-carbon generation.

## Current Valuation Multiples

Exact share-price data at the precise snapshot date warrants a methodological note: the following figures are reasoned from Constellation's last-reported share count and the price range derivable from available filings and press releases. The January 2025 Calpine acquisition announcement attributed approximately $10.2 billion in equity value to the roughly 50 million CEG shares to be issued to Calpine shareholders — implying a deal reference price of approximately $204 per share at announcement. Subsequent earnings releases through the first half of 2025 and the visible price range from public reporting suggest CEG traded in the approximate range of $220–$270 through available windows. Applying that range to the approximately 330 million shares outstanding prior to the Calpine close produces a market capitalisation estimate in the vicinity of $73–$89 billion.

Against fiscal 2024 adjusted EBITDA of approximately [$4.8 billion](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/financial-information), that implies a trailing EV/EBITDA of roughly 18–22x — assuming net debt in the low-to-mid single-digit billions from Constellation's standalone balance sheet, before Calpine's approximately $12.7 billion in assumed net debt is consolidated. On a forward basis, analyst consensus heading into 2025 priced in meaningful EBITDA step-ups from elevated [PJM capacity revenues](https://www.pjm.com) (the July 2024 capacity auction cleared at over $269/MW-day for most of the footprint), incremental hyperscaler PPA monetisation, and, following the Calpine close, roughly 15–20 percent EBITDA accretion from the combined platform. A forward EV/EBITDA in the 14–17x range on 2026 estimates, post-Calpine and pre-synergy, is a reasonable read of where the market settled through the reporting windows available.

Price-to-earnings multiples for merchant power companies with variable nuclear production tax credit treatment are somewhat less informative as a primary metric; nonetheless, on consensus after-tax adjusted earnings in the $8–$10 per share range for the forward period, the stock's implied P/E sits in the 25–32x range — well above sector medians, and indicative of the growth premium the market attached to the AI electricity demand thesis.

## Historical Re-Rating: From Spin Discount to Infrastructure Premium

The contrast with Constellation's 2022 listing is instructive. In its first full year as a standalone entity, CEG traded between approximately $30 and $65 per share, implying a market capitalisation that barely exceeded $10–$15 billion and an EV/EBITDA in the 5–8x range. That multiple reflected genuine structural risk: merchant nuclear operators carried commodity power price exposure without the regulatory return guarantees of their utility-model peers, and the economics of operating ageing reactors in competitive wholesale markets had historically been severe enough that Exelon had sought — and in Illinois obtained — ratepayer-funded subsidies to keep the fleet commercially viable.

The re-rating unfolded in three distinct phases. The IRA's passage in August 2022 provided the first catalyst: Section 45U installed a statutory floor on nuclear revenue exposure, materially improving the risk-return calculus and enabling Constellation to project long-term cash flows with a confidence impossible under pre-IRA merchant economics. The second phase — arguably the more dramatic — began with the [September 20 2024 announcement](https://investors.constellationenergy.com) of the Microsoft 20-year power purchase agreement at the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1. That single transaction demonstrated that hyperscalers would pay structurally premium prices for firm, zero-carbon nuclear gigawatt-hours, transforming Constellation from a commodity generator into a contracted infrastructure asset in the market's assessment. The stock roughly quadrupled from its 2022 lows to the levels implied at the Calpine announcement reference price. The third phase — still developing as of the snapshot — is the prospective consolidation trade: whether the Calpine combination creates sufficient EBITDA scale and geographic diversification to sustain a premium multiple against a materially larger denominator.

## Peer Group Multiple Comparison

The table below benchmarks Constellation's estimated multiples against a selected peer group as of the snapshot window. All figures are approximate and sourced from available public filings and market reporting; they should be read as indicative ranges rather than point estimates.

| Company | Ticker | Forward EV/EBITDA | Trailing P/E | Primary Business Mix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Constellation Energy | CEG | 14–17x | 25–32x | Nuclear pure-play + gas/geothermal (Calpine) |
| Vistra Energy | VST | 11–14x | 20–26x | Merchant power: nuclear, gas, battery storage |
| Talen Energy | TLN | 9–12x | 15–20x | Nuclear pure-play (smaller scale) |
| NRG Energy | NRG | 8–11x | 14–18x | Merchant retail and wholesale, gas-fired |
| PSEG | PEG | 10–13x | 18–22x | Regulated utility plus contracted nuclear operation |
| NextEra Energy | NEE | 13–16x | 22–28x | Regulated utility plus contracted renewables |

Constellation's premium to Vistra — its closest true peer in the merchant nuclear and AI data centre electricity narrative — is notable. Both companies benefit from similar demand-side tailwinds and comparable IRA credit structures, but Constellation's scale advantage (approximately 22 GW of nuclear capacity versus Vistra's smaller nuclear footprint), the specific commercial credibility of the Microsoft TMI PPA as a template transaction, and the longer weighted-average contract life on hyperscaler offtake appeared to command a genuine valuation differential. The premium to Talen reflects the scale gap and the perception that Constellation's diversified multi-region fleet reduces concentration risk. The premium to regulated utilities such as PSEG and NextEra reflects the market's current preference for the higher-growth, unregulated nuclear story over rate-base utility compounding — a meaningful reversal of the traditional utility premium to merchant generation that persisted for most of the prior decade.

## Intrinsic Value and Cash Flow Implied by Current Price

A simplified scenario-based framework anchors the market's embedded assumptions. Applying a 10 percent discount rate to the combined post-Calpine platform — with consensus 2026 EBITDA in the $7–$9 billion range, comprising Constellation's standalone run-rate plus Calpine's contribution and ahead of meaningful synergy realisation — and assuming a 12–14x terminal EV/EBITDA multiple reflecting a normalised merchant power market, produces a fair-value range of roughly $180–$240 per share. At the upper end of the implied traded range (~$270), the market was effectively assuming one or more of the following: material synergy realisation above the baseline management framework, additional hyperscaler PPA transactions at TMI-equivalent economics, power prices sustaining above current forward curves, or a durable multiple premium as AI power infrastructure becomes a recognised institutional asset class. None of these assumptions is implausible in isolation; in combination, they represent a compounding of favourable outcomes that warrants scrutiny.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Valuation Scenarios

**Bull scenario — $320–$380 per share.** The bull case assumes the Calpine integration closes cleanly in the second half of 2025, synergies track toward the high end of management's disclosed framework, and two to three additional hyperscaler PPAs at pricing equivalent to or modestly below the Microsoft TMI template are signed and disclosed before year-end 2026. Power forward curves in PJM and ERCOT remain elevated, sustained by AI data centre load growth. Section 45U continues to operate as designed through the IRA's scheduled horizon to 2032. On these assumptions, a 16–18x forward EV/EBITDA multiple on $8.5–$9.5 billion of combined 2027 EBITDA produces an equity value in the $320–$380 range. The implicit forward P/E at this level — roughly 30–38x — is aggressive by historical power sector standards but defensible if consensus re-classifies Constellation as an infrastructure compounder rather than a commodity generator.

**Base scenario — $230–$270 per share.** The base case holds current power forward curves broadly stable, the Calpine close delivers on the lower-to-mid range of disclosed synergy targets ($400–$500 million over three years), and one additional major hyperscaler PPA is signed during the 2025–2026 window. Section 45U remains intact. Combined 2027 EBITDA of $7.5–$8.5 billion at 13–15x forward EV/EBITDA produces an implied equity range of $230–$270 — broadly in line with where the stock traded through the 2025 reporting windows derivable from available public data. This is the consensus-tracking scenario, and the one most directly reflected in sell-side price targets visible through the snapshot window.

**Bear scenario — $130–$170 per share.** The bear case does not require catastrophe; it requires normalisation. If power prices soften materially — whether from a slower-than-expected AI buildout, accelerated renewable interconnection into constrained zones, or demand-side response — Section 45U provides support but is insufficient to sustain a premium multiple absent growth optionality. Calpine integration friction, adverse FERC rulings on market structure, or delays to the Crane Clean Energy Center NRC re-licensing process could each add meaningful execution risk. On $6–$7 billion of combined EBITDA at 9–11x forward EV/EBITDA, the equity compresses to $130–$170. This range implies roughly a 40–50 percent drawdown from the top of the implied current trading band, reflecting a compression of the AI demand premium back toward historical merchant power multiples — painful, but not existential for a business backed by Section 45U and PJM capacity payments.

## What the Market Is Currently Pricing In

The gap between the bear scenario and the current trading range represents the market's explicit bet that AI data centre electricity demand constitutes a durable structural shift rather than a cyclical demand spike. As of the snapshot date, that bet appears well-founded: hyperscaler capital expenditure commitments, NRC licence extension activity, and the PJM interconnection queue composition all reinforce the directional thesis. The more nuanced question is whether the specific nuclear premium — the market's belief that Constellation's zero-carbon, firm-capacity offering commands a structural price above alternative generation technologies — survives potential entry of small modular reactors at scale, multi-day battery storage at competitive economics, or long-duration geothermal buildout reaching commercial maturity within the 45U horizon. The dossier's read is that the base scenario is appropriately priced at current levels, the bull scenario is plausible but requires sequential execution on Calpine integration, hyperscaler contracting, and the TMI restart simultaneously, and the bear scenario — while not the consensus — represents a more credible tail than the current multiple implies. At two-to-three turns EV/EBITDA above Vistra and four-to-five turns above NRG, Constellation's equity has already captured the first-mover narrative. The question as of 23 May 2026 is whether it can grow into it.

chapters.title: From the 2022 post-spin baseline to the 2024 record and Calpine
chapters.body:
## Standing Alone: Q1 2022 and the Post-Spin Thesis

On February 1, 2022, Constellation Energy Corporation became a publicly traded company on NASDAQ under the ticker CEG, completing its separation from Exelon Corporation after Exelon's board determined that the merchant generation business warranted its own equity identity. The spin deposited into the public markets the largest nuclear fleet operator in the United States — approximately 22 gigawatts across twelve sites and more than twenty-one reactors — without the earnings-smoothing backstop of a regulated utility parent.

Joe Dominguez, installed as president and chief executive at the moment of separation, used the first post-spin earnings cycle to frame what Constellation was, and what it was not. The company was not a regulated utility earning a predictable return on equity filed with a state commission. It was a merchant generator in a competitive wholesale market — a distinction that the pre-IRA nuclear sector had spent a decade being punished for. Dominguez and CFO Daniel Eggers, who had joined in December 2021 specifically in anticipation of the separation, presented a clean-energy baseload thesis: Constellation's nuclear output was, by output volume, the largest source of carbon-free electricity in the United States, and the policy environment was tilting, at last, in its favour.

Revenue in the first full post-spin fiscal year, 2022, reached $24.4 billion, reflecting the elevated power-price environment of a year in which European natural gas dislocations rippled through US wholesale electricity markets. Adjusted EBITDA for 2022 came in at approximately $2.7 billion — a respectable first year, but one that masked an important structural constraint: the pre-IRA merchant nuclear model required power prices to remain elevated to justify continued operation of older units across the fleet. That constraint was about to be removed.

## The IRA and the 45U Floor: August 2022 Transforms the Risk Profile

The Inflation Reduction Act, signed in August 2022, contained at Section 45U a production tax credit for existing nuclear generation that fundamentally altered the investment calculus for Constellation and, by extension, for the US merchant nuclear sector broadly. The credit provided up to $15 per megawatt-hour, subject to an income-level phase-out triggered when effective plant revenues exceeded approximately $25 per MWh, and applied through tax year 2032.

The economic implication was structural rather than incidental. At low power prices — the scenario that had periodically threatened uneconomic plant closures in the pre-IRA era — the 45U credit stepped in to underwrite a floor on effective nuclear revenue. At elevated power prices the credit phased down or out, but in that environment the merchant exposure itself was the value driver. Constellation's hedging and operating teams spent the second half of 2022 and much of 2023 working through implementation mechanics with Treasury, while Dominguez made the case in investor forums and on earnings calls that the IRA had converted the nuclear fleet from an uncertain merchant survivor into a structurally insulated generator with a policy-backstopped floor.

The financial trajectory through fiscal 2023 reflected the early harvest of that re-rating. Revenue came in at $23.6 billion — slightly below the elevated 2022 figure as power markets normalised from the gas-price spike — but adjusted EBITDA jumped to $3.8 billion, an increase of more than forty percent over the 2022 post-spin baseline. The EBITDA expansion in the face of flat revenue revealed the operating-leverage dynamic at work: the IRA 45U credit was flowing through to the bottom line, and the fleet's nuclear production efficiency was holding firm across the operating base.

By the time Eggers and Dominguez discussed Q4 2023 results in February 2024, the AI narrative was beginning to surface explicitly in earnings commentary. The hyperscaler demand thesis — major technology companies seeking large-scale commitments of firm, carbon-free electricity to power data centre build-outs — had circulated in energy analyst circles for several quarters, and Constellation was fielding inbound interest from potential counterparties. The company's ability to offer gigawatt-scale, carbon-free, around-the-clock nuclear baseload from a fleet already interconnected across PJM, MISO, and other major grid regions made it structurally positioned for the emerging corporate PPA market in a way no wind or solar developer could match.

## September 20, 2024: Three Mile Island and the Microsoft Transaction

The principal inflection event of Constellation's post-spin history arrived on September 20, 2024, when the company announced a twenty-year power purchase agreement with Microsoft for the full output of a restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1 — the 835-megawatt reactor that had been shut down in 2019. [Constellation Energy IR](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/financial-information) Constellation committed approximately $1.6 billion to the restart programme, encompassing refurbishment and NRC re-licensing costs, with a target restart date of 2028. The facility was renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, honouring former Exelon chief executive Chris Crane.

The transaction was transformative on several dimensions simultaneously. It demonstrated that a hyperscaler with the scale and creditworthiness of Microsoft was prepared to commit to a twenty-year nuclear power contract — an instrument that, prior to 2024, had no precedent in US commercial nuclear history. It validated the carbon-free, around-the-clock premium that nuclear generation commands over intermittent renewables for data centre customers operating against Science Based Targets and aggressive Scope 2 commitments. And it established a pricing and structural template — long tenor, take-or-pay economics, investment-grade counterparty — that the Constellation commercial organisation under Chief Commercial Officer James McHugh could reference in every subsequent hyperscaler negotiation.

In Q3 2024 earnings commentary, Dominguez characterised the Microsoft transaction as a defining moment not merely for Constellation but for the US nuclear industry broadly — confirmation that the fleet's economic life could be extended and monetised through commercial PPA structures at prices that fully justified the capital commitment. Eggers, in concurrent investor presentations, highlighted the transaction's contribution to the fleet's long-term revenue-visibility profile, framing the 20-year Microsoft commitment as the opening data point in what he expected to become a growing portfolio of similar agreements.

The market agreed with the framing. CEG shares re-rated materially through the second half of 2024, making Constellation one of the best-performing US large-cap equities of the year. The stock's journey from its February 2022 post-spin baseline had been a slow accumulation of thesis-confirmatory data points — the IRA enactment, the 45U Treasury guidance, the AI demand narrative building in analyst commentary — but the Microsoft PPA was the event that triggered a step-change in institutional conviction.

## FY2024 Record Results and the Calpine Announcement

The Q4 2024 and full-year earnings release, published in February 2025, confirmed the scale of the earnings inflection. Full-year 2024 revenue held approximately flat at $23.6 billion — consistent with fiscal 2023 — while adjusted EBITDA reached $4.8 billion, an increase of roughly $1.0 billion over the prior year and nearly double the 2022 post-spin baseline.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD bn) | Adj. EBITDA (USD bn) | EBITDA Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 (first full post-spin year) | 24.4 | 2.7 | 11.1% |
| 2023 | 23.6 | 3.8 | 16.1% |
| 2024 | 23.6 | 4.8 | 20.3% |

The margin expansion — from 11.1 percent of revenue in 2022 to 20.3 percent in 2024 — was the product of three reinforcing forces: the 45U PTC providing a floor at lower-price nodes, the elevated PJM capacity market clearing in the July 2024 base-residual auction (above $269 per MW-day across the majority of PJM's footprint, with constrained zones materially higher), and the initial commercial premium embedded in the hyperscaler PPA structure at Three Mile Island.

The February 2025 earnings release came with a major strategic transaction already in place: on January 10, 2025, Constellation had announced the acquisition of Calpine Corporation for total consideration of approximately $26.6 billion — comprising roughly $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million CEG shares (valued at approximately $10.2 billion at announcement), and the assumption of approximately $12.7 billion of Calpine net debt. Calpine, the largest US private power producer, owned by Energy Capital Partners, Access Industries, and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, brought approximately 27 gigawatts of principally gas-fired capacity spanning ERCOT and CAISO, plus the Geysers geothermal portfolio in California.

The strategic logic was both defensive and offensive. Dispatchable gas-fired capacity addressed a structural criticism of the pure-play nuclear model: nuclear is baseload, not peaking, and the highest-marginal-value power-market hours are peak-demand events that gas plants are designed to serve. Adding Calpine gave Constellation a dispatchable fleet to layer against the nuclear baseload, strengthening its product offering to hyperscaler customers seeking round-the-clock reliability plus peak-hour coverage. ERCOT and CAISO exposure diversified the company away from its heavy PJM concentration, expanding the addressable commercial market into two of the three largest US power pools. The Geysers geothermal portfolio added firm, carbon-free generation of a type hyperscalers could include in their clean-energy accounting alongside the nuclear baseload.

## 2025 and the Broadening Pipeline

Through 2025 and into Q1 2026, Constellation's earnings communications focused on three interlocking themes: Calpine regulatory approval and integration progress; the broadening hyperscaler PPA pipeline beyond the initial Microsoft TMI transaction; and the ongoing Section 45U PTC realisation across the full fleet.

The Calpine transaction, targeting closure in late 2025 or early 2026 subject to FERC, NRC, and Calpine shareholder approval, dominated the structural narrative on investor days and earnings calls. Dominguez framed the combined platform — nuclear baseload plus gas-fired peaking plus geothermal firm renewable — as a uniquely comprehensive US merchant power portfolio capable of meeting the full spectrum of hyperscaler electricity needs across the load-shape and carbon-attribute dimensions that large technology-company procurement teams required.

The 45U PTC, having cleared its final Treasury guidance iterations, was flowing through the annual tax provision on the schedule Congress had intended. Eggers's communications through 2025 addressed the credit's interaction with the growing commercial PPA portfolio — specifically, how contracted prices above the phase-out threshold affected the realised value of the 45U floor at individual plants — as the fleet's effective blended price per MWh continued to rise with each incremental hyperscaler agreement added to the book.

The earnings arc from the February 2022 post-spin baseline through Q1 2026 described a company that had navigated from an uncertain merchant survivor — trading at a discount to regulated utility peers precisely because of its unhedged nuclear exposure — into the principal equity instrument for the AI data centre electricity investment thesis. Adjusted EBITDA had nearly doubled across two fiscal years. The twenty-year Microsoft PPA had unlocked a commercial template replicable across other units in the 22-gigawatt fleet. The Calpine acquisition had elevated the company into a categorically different scale class of US power producer. And the IRA Section 45U floor had permanently removed the downside tail risk that had historically suppressed the merchant nuclear equity multiple.

chapters.title: Dominguez, Shattuck, Eggers, and the nuclear-operator board
