## Dominguez at the helm: the CEO mandate

When Exelon Corporation completed the February 1, 2022 separation that created Constellation Energy Corporation, Joseph Dominguez inherited a peculiar mandate: build a coherent identity for a company that was simultaneously the largest US nuclear fleet operator, a competitive retail electricity supplier, and a merchant generation business whose earnings were structurally correlated to commodity power prices. The CEO role required fluency across regulatory affairs, nuclear operations, and the increasingly complex world of merchant power markets.

Dominguez was, in most respects, a natural fit. A mechanical engineer by training from the New Jersey Institute of Technology, he had later taken a law degree *magna cum laude* from Rutgers before spending years as an assistant US attorney in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. His energy career was built at Exelon across the regulatory and government affairs function — he served as EVP for governmental and regulatory affairs before becoming chief executive of ComEd, Exelon's Illinois transmission and distribution subsidiary serving more than four million customers in the Chicago metropolitan area.

What the ComEd tenure gave Dominguez was precisely the stakeholder management and political engagement that merchant power generation requires. Nuclear relicensing, capacity market design advocacy at FERC, state zero-emission credit programmes, and ultimately the IRA Section 45U production tax credit negotiation — all involved the same combination of regulatory command and political coalition-building that had defined his regulated-utility years. At the September 2024 announcement of the Crane Clean Energy Center restart and the Microsoft twenty-year power purchase agreement, Dominguez articulated the commercial thesis plainly:

> "The agreement marks the dawn of a new era of nuclear energy. It demonstrates nuclear's capability to meet the demands of our modern economy and confirms our belief that nuclear energy is essential to a clean energy future."

The Microsoft transaction also illustrated how dramatically the CEO role at Constellation had expanded beyond fleet management. By early 2025, Dominguez was simultaneously managing the company's position on nuclear policy, its engagement with hyperscaler customers across multiple emerging PPA structures, its capital allocation between fleet investment and shareholder returns, and from January 2025 the complexity of acquiring Calpine Corporation — a $26.6 billion all-in transaction that would transform the fleet from a nuclear pure-play into the largest competitive power generator in the United States.

## The CFO function: Eggers, Smith, and the capital structure trajectory

Daniel Eggers joined Constellation Energy as chief financial officer in December 2021, several weeks before the February 2022 spin. His background was unusual among US utility and power company CFOs: approximately eighteen years at Credit Suisse, where he co-headed US energy equity research and built deep coverage of both regulated utilities and independent power producers, before moving to Exelon's investor relations and corporate finance function. That analytical heritage made him an unusually adept communicator with the institutional investor base — in three consecutive years he won [Institutional Investor](https://www.institutionalinvestor.com)'s best CFO award for the utilities sector (2023, 2024, and 2025), an acknowledgement both of shareholder returns and of his visible presence in the capital markets narrative.

The post-spin capital structure work fell squarely on Eggers's desk: the dividend initiation, successive share repurchase programmes, and the management of the Section 45U production tax credit as a structural earnings floor on commodity power exposure. With the closing of the Calpine acquisition in January 2026, Eggers transitioned to a newly created role as Senior Executive Vice President for Finance and Data Economy — a title that acknowledged both the expanded balance sheet and the company's emerging commercial ambitions in AI data centre energy solutions as a distinct revenue line. Shane Smith, who had spent twenty years in the Constellation and Exelon finance organisation and had led treasury and credit through the Calpine deal structuring, ascended to the CFO seat. The Smith promotion maintained the internal continuity culture that had characterised management succession across the post-spin period.

## The operational core

Bryan Hanson, as Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Generation Officer, carried the company's largest single operational responsibility: the safe and reliable operation of more than 170 generating units coast-to-coast, anchored by the twenty-plus nuclear reactors that produce the majority of Constellation's earnings. Hanson's career had been spent almost entirely within nuclear operations — beginning at the plant level, extending through fleet-wide oversight at Exelon Nuclear before the spin, and reaching the executive leadership position that now encompassed the post-Calpine generation portfolio including gas and geothermal assets. He chaired the 2025 American Nuclear Society Annual Conference, reflecting his standing in the broader US nuclear operating community.

James McHugh, as Chief Commercial Officer, ran the organisation through which the hyperscaler PPA framework was developed and executed. McHugh had spent the bulk of his career in the Constellation commercial machine: he previously served as CEO of the Constellation subsidiary within Exelon Generation, and before that held senior wholesale trading and portfolio management roles dating to the early Exelon Power Team years. His engineering degree from Lehigh and MBA in finance from Villanova framed a career that combined power-systems technical depth with commercial structuring competence. The Microsoft PPA was the most visible output of the commercial organisation, but McHugh's team simultaneously managed wholesale hedging across the PJM, MISO, NYISO, and ISO-NE footprints and built the pipeline of subsequent hyperscaler PPA engagements that the company flagged as pipeline through 2025.

Kathleen Barron, as Executive Vice President and Senior Advisor to the CEO, brought thirty years of energy policy and regulatory law to the executive committee. She had served as Deputy General Counsel at FERC — advising the Commission on organised electric market design and representing FERC before Congress — before joining Constellation's predecessor in 2010. Her fifteen years in the company's government and regulatory affairs function made her the principal architect of the engagement at the NRC, FERC, and across state regulatory bodies that contributed to the IRA nuclear provisions taking their final form. Barron announced plans to retire in 2026 after three decades in the industry, representing an eventual transition point for the public policy function.

David Dardis, as Chief External Affairs and Growth Officer, combined legal leadership with new development activity. A Pomona and Washington & Lee Law graduate, Dardis had served as legal adviser to FERC Chairman Joseph Kelliher during the implementation of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 and the development of the agency's enforcement programme before joining Constellation's predecessor in 2007. His nearly two decades in the organisation encompassed complex M&A execution including the Calpine transaction, major commercial contract negotiations, government investigations, and sustained national energy policy advocacy.

## The board: expertise calibrated to a merchant nuclear business

The Constellation Energy board assembled at the February 2022 spin carried a disciplined composition logic: technical nuclear expertise, financial markets depth, large industrial operating experience, and regulatory familiarity — with none of the conventions that typically dominate a regulated transmission-and-distribution company's governance structure.

**Robert J. Lawless** served as non-executive Chairman, and his tenure with the Constellation enterprise was longer than virtually any other current board member. Lawless had first joined the Constellation Energy Group board in 2002 — a full decade before the original group merged into Exelon — and had continued on the Exelon board through the 2022 separation, arriving at the new CEG as Chairman at inception. His operating career was as Chairman, President, and CEO of McCormick & Company, the Fortune 500 spice and flavoring manufacturer: a background that brought large-enterprise operational governance discipline rather than sector-specific nuclear expertise, paired with twenty-plus years of direct institutional memory of the Constellation and Exelon nuclear-fleet businesses across multiple market cycles.

**Yves C. de Balmann** brought the deepest capital markets pedigree on the board. He served as Co-Head of Deutsche Bank's Global Investment Bank and as Co-Chairman and Co-CEO of BT Alex. Brown — the bulge-bracket investment banking operation within Bankers Trust — before building Bregal Investments, a private equity platform for the Brenninkmeijer family, from inception to more than €18 billion in assets under management. Critically, de Balmann also served on the original Constellation Energy Group board from 2003 to 2012, giving him direct prior exposure to the merchant nuclear business before it became part of Exelon. He chaired the Compensation Committee and sat on Corporate Governance. As the company navigated the Calpine financing structure, the hyperscaler PPA economics, and the evolving capital return programme, his transactional and capital markets depth was structurally relevant in ways that few other board members could replicate.

**Admiral John M. Richardson** provided the board's most direct nuclear technical oversight. Richardson served as the 31st Chief of Naval Operations — the highest-ranking officer in the US Navy — and before that as Director of Naval Reactors, the position responsible for the full life-cycle management and regulatory compliance of more than ninety reactors aboard nuclear-powered warships. The combination of engineering credentials (physics at the Naval Academy; electrical engineering at MIT and Woods Hole) with regulatory experience managing a naval nuclear fleet larger than any commercial operator made him uniquely qualified to chair the Nuclear Oversight Committee — the standing committee with direct responsibility over Constellation's fleet safety programme.

**Dhiaa Jamil** complemented Richardson's credentials with commercial utility nuclear operations experience. Jamil spent forty-one years at Duke Energy, rising to Chief Nuclear Officer overseeing the largest regulated nuclear fleet in the country before serving as Chief Operating Officer until his 2023 retirement. His direct management of the Duke-Progress Energy nuclear integration — twelve units across two organisations — provided a merger-integration reference that was relevant as Constellation absorbed the Calpine fleet. He served on both the Compensation and Nuclear Oversight committees.

**Bradley M. Halverson** chaired the Audit and Risk Committee. His operating background was as Group President and CFO of Caterpillar — a Fortune 100 capital-intensive industrial company with global treasury, financial reporting, and risk management complexity. His public accounting origins at Price Waterhouse, combined with his ongoing audit committee chairmanship at Sysco Corporation, provided technical financial governance depth.

**Charles L. Harrington** served as Corporate Governance Committee Chair with a career that combined engineering and technology leadership with large organisation management. As Chairman, CEO, and President of Parsons Corporation, he oversaw cybersecurity, national security contracting, and complex critical infrastructure programmes directly relevant to Constellation's nuclear regulatory environment and broader infrastructure positioning.

**Julie Holzrichter** brought risk management and large-scale systems experience from her decade as Chief Operating Officer of CME Group, the world's leading derivatives marketplace. Operational risk, regulatory compliance, technology platform management, and the integration of multiple multi-billion-dollar exchange acquisitions during her CME tenure mapped onto Constellation's trading, retail, and risk management businesses.

**Ashish Khandpur** joined the board from a career in advanced materials and industrial technology, including the Research and Development leadership and CTO role at 3M Corporation, and subsequently the CEO and Chairman position at Avient Corporation. His innovation and technology orientation was increasingly relevant as Constellation sought to articulate its positioning in the AI data centre energy ecosystem.

**Eileen Paterson** arrived in December 2024 with aerospace and defence operating credentials — she had been CEO of Aerojet Rocketdyne, a major defence propulsion company — and brought a US Army aviation background that added an operational dimension distinct from the finance and industrial profiles elsewhere on the board. She served on the Nuclear Oversight and Corporate Governance committees.

**Nneka Rimmer** brought strategy consulting depth — fifteen years at Boston Consulting Group, where she became the firm's first Black female partner — alongside operational experience as President of McCormick's Global Flavors and Extracts division and chief transformation officer of the same business. Her M&A advisory and execution track record, including the largest acquisition in McCormick history, was directly applicable to a board overseeing a $26.6 billion integration.

## Composition thesis

Read as an ensemble, the board's composition reflected neither the regulatory-compact heritage of a traditional investor-owned utility nor the financial-engineering orientation of a private equity-backed merchant generator. It was instead calibrated to the specific demands of a post-2022 nuclear pure-play: technical oversight of an operationally complex and heavily regulated nuclear fleet (Richardson, Jamil, Paterson); financial and transactional governance of a merchant business with large capital market exposure (de Balmann, Halverson, Holzrichter); industrial operating depth (Harrington, Khandpur, Rimmer); and a Chairman in Lawless whose two decades of Constellation-enterprise board experience provided institutional continuity across every structural iteration of the business since the Constellation Energy Group's independent years. The Nuclear Oversight Committee — a standing committee with no equivalent on most large-cap corporate boards — was itself a structural statement about where the business's operational risks resided. The post-Calpine board carried the same logic, extended to a generation fleet that now encompassed gas and geothermal assets alongside the nuclear core that remained the earnings foundation.

chapters.title: Microsoft, hyperscalers, C&I customers, and the nuclear fuel cycle
chapters.body:
## The Crane Clean Energy Center: Microsoft and the Commercial Template

On September 20, 2024, Constellation Energy announced that it would restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 — the reactor idle since 2019 — and sell its entire output to Microsoft under a twenty-year power purchase agreement. The announcement crystallised a thesis that had been forming across the power industry: that the AI data centre build-out had created structural demand for always-available, zero-carbon baseload electricity that only nuclear generation could reliably supply. No other commodity could satisfy what the hyperscalers were beginning to call a "24/7 carbon-free" requirement at the gigawatt scale.

The plant, rechristened the Crane Clean Energy Center in honour of former Exelon chief executive Chris Crane, carries 835 megawatts of nameplate capacity. Constellation committed approximately $1.6 billion to the restart programme, covering refurbishment of the turbine hall and supporting systems, regulatory compliance upgrades, and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission re-licensing process. The company subsequently accelerated its operational target to mid-2027, earlier than the original 2028 horizon, after the NRC indicated it expected to complete its licence review by 2027. In November 2025, the Trump administration deepened the federal backing: the Department of Energy closed a $1 billion conditional loan under the Title XVII clean-energy finance programme, with the first advance scheduled for the first quarter of 2026, covering the majority of the restart capital outlay. The DOE described the Crane transaction as the first project to achieve concurrent conditional commitment and financial close under the new administration, framing it explicitly as a national-security energy infrastructure investment.

Joe Dominguez, Constellation's chief executive, argued that the commercial logic was straightforward. Hyperscalers required power that was simultaneously continuous, carbon-accountable, and physically located within the same grid region as their data centres. Describing the competitive position of nuclear generation, he stated:

> "Powering industries critical to our nation's global economic and technological competitiveness, including data centers, requires an abundance of energy that is carbon-free and reliable every hour of every day, and nuclear plants are the only energy sources that can consistently deliver on that promise."

Microsoft's contracting structure for the Crane centre reflected that logic. The twenty-year PPA runs against the full 835-megawatt output of the facility, sized to serve power consumption across Microsoft's PJM-region data centre portfolio. The deal provided Constellation with a long-dated, investment-grade counterparty revenue guarantee against which to justify the restart capital — and it gave Microsoft a carbon accounting instrument far more robust than renewable energy certificates from wind or solar, whose generation profiles are intermittent and locationally diffuse.

## Meta and the Expanding Hyperscaler Pipeline

The Crane PPA proved to be the template rather than the exception. On June 3, 2025, Constellation and Meta announced a separate twenty-year power purchase agreement covering the full output of the Clinton Clean Energy Center in central Illinois — a 1,121-megawatt pressurised water reactor that had operated on state-funded zero-emission credits under Illinois's nuclear support programme. The ZEC framework, which had sustained the plant's economics through competitive electricity price weakness, was approaching expiration. The Meta agreement replaced the ratepayer-funded subsidy with a direct hyperscaler off-take commitment, extending Clinton's operating life by two decades on a purely market-based footing.

The Clinton PPA carries several structural features that illustrate how hyperscaler counterparties are adapting the standard corporate PPA format to nuclear baseload. The agreement begins in June 2027 — timed to the anticipated expiration of the ZEC contracts — and it incorporates a 30-megawatt capacity uprate at the plant, lifting total output above the original nameplate. Constellation estimated that the deal would preserve approximately 1,100 direct jobs at the Clinton site, contribute $13.5 million in annual local tax revenue, and include $1 million in community charitable commitments over five years. Dominguez characterised the agreement as "a model for how America's clean energy future can be driven by partnerships with forward-thinking companies."

Beyond Microsoft and Meta, Dominguez signalled in multiple earnings communications through 2025 that the hyperscaler dialogue had broadened materially. On the Q2 2025 call, he cited projections showing hyperscaler capital expenditure on data centre infrastructure for 2026 running approximately 75 percent above the prior year's pace. Constellation responded by submitting approximately 5,000 megawatts of new capacity resources into PJM's generation interconnection queue — a combination of nuclear uprates at existing plants, new natural gas peakers, and battery storage — positioning the fleet to serve additional off-take commitments as negotiations progressed. Dominguez noted a preference for announcing concluded data centre agreements in the presence of local community stakeholders rather than disclosing on earnings calls, suggesting additional executed PPAs may have preceded formal public announcement. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the Microsoft and Meta agreements represented the two publicly confirmed hyperscaler bilateral PPAs in Constellation's portfolio.

## PJM and the Wholesale Capacity Premium

Beyond the bilateral hyperscaler channel, Constellation's nuclear fleet captures substantial revenue from PJM Interconnection's capacity market — the mechanism through which the grid operator procures the committed generation needed to meet peak demand with a defined reliability margin. The combination of retiring coal capacity, surging AI data centre load, and sluggish new-build entry has produced three consecutive capacity auction records in PJM, each driven in part by the same demand signal that has animated the hyperscaler PPA market.

The 2025–2026 delivery-year Base Residual Auction cleared at $269.92 per megawatt-day across the RTO — approximately five times the depressed clearing levels of several years prior. The subsequent 2026–2027 auction, results of which were published on July 22, 2025, cleared at $329.17 per megawatt-day, a 22 percent increase representing a third consecutive record high, as PJM's own forecast showed peak load for the 2026–2027 year rising by more than 5,400 megawatts year-on-year, driven explicitly by data centre expansion and industrial electrification. Constellation's nuclear units — which cleared 21 percent of PJM's total procured capacity across the resource mix — captured those prices across the fleet.

The December 2025 auction for the 2027–2028 delivery year was particularly significant for Constellation's forward revenue visibility: the company disclosed in its associated 8-K filing that it had cleared approximately 17,950 megawatts of capacity, translating to approximately $2.2 billion in committed capacity revenues for that delivery year. These contracted capacity revenues, stacked atop the bilateral hyperscaler PPAs and the IRA Section 45U production tax credit floor of up to $15 per megawatt-hour on energy revenue, constructed a multi-layered revenue architecture that was qualitatively different from the merchant nuclear economics of the pre-IRA era.

## Commercial and Industrial Supply: The Retail Foundation

Constellation's generation assets sit atop a retail and wholesale supply business that predates the February 2022 spin from Exelon and traces its heritage to the legacy Constellation Energy Group competitive supply operation. As of the spin-off, the competitive supply business was serving approximately 140 terawatt-hours of electric power load and approximately 800 billion cubic feet of natural gas annually, principally to commercial and industrial customers across the deregulated states of the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, and Northeast — markets where retail customers may choose their power supplier outside the regulated utility default service.

The C&I customer base spans Fortune 100 manufacturers, hospital systems, universities, municipalities, and government entities concentrated in states including Maryland, Pennsylvania, Illinois, New York, New Jersey, and Ohio. Constellation's value proposition to these customers combines physical supply from the nuclear fleet — zero-carbon, baseload electricity with demonstrable hourly matching — with the financial and structured products capacity of the competitive supply organisation. This retail channel operates in parallel to the hyperscaler PPA business and provides a diversification of counterparty credit quality and tenor. It also serves as a commercial intelligence channel: the company's direct relationships with large industrial consumers give it early visibility into load-growth signals from manufacturing expansions, electrification programmes, and — increasingly — the mid-tier data centre operators who have not yet reached the scale of hyperscaler counterparts.

## The Nuclear Fuel Cycle: Concentration, Geopolitics, and the Russian Equation

Operating the largest US nuclear fleet generates a procurement footprint that extends from the uranium mines of Kazakhstan, Canada, and Australia through conversion plants, enrichment facilities, and fuel fabrication shops before arriving at the reactor core. Each stage of the fuel cycle carries its own supply-concentration risk, and the geopolitical dislocation triggered by Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine threw the enrichment segment specifically into relief.

Russian state-controlled enrichment capacity, operated through Rosatom's TENEX and TVEL subsidiaries, had supplied approximately 20 percent of enriched uranium delivered to US reactors as recently as 2024, reflecting long-term supply contracts negotiated over decades. The Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act, signed into law on May 13, 2024, established a statutory ban on imports of Russian-origin low-enriched uranium, effective 90 days after enactment — approximately August 2024 — while authorising the Department of Energy to grant national-interest waivers through 2028 where no alternative supply was available. Constellation Energy, alongside Centrus Energy, was among the entities that secured such waivers, reflecting the material time required to redirect enrichment requirements to Western suppliers.

The Western enrichment landscape is effectively a three-provider oligopoly: Centrus Energy (formerly USEC), which operates the American Centrifuge Plant in Piketon, Ohio; Urenco, a British-German-Dutch consortium with US enrichment capacity at the Louisiana Energy Services facility in New Mexico; and Orano (formerly Areva), a French state-backed group with global enrichment infrastructure. Centrus has been scaling domestic centrifuge manufacturing with backing from the Department of Energy's civil nuclear programme and a February 2025 supply contract with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power; it delivered over 920 kilograms of high-assay low-enriched uranium to the DOE through mid-2025 as part of a demonstration programme for next-generation reactor fuel.

The downstream fuel fabrication step — where enriched uranium hexafluoride is converted into ceramic pellets and assembled into fuel assemblies — is dominated in the US by Westinghouse Electric Company, which supplies light-water reactor fuel for Constellation's pressurised and boiling water units, and by Framatome (formerly Areva NP), which serves portions of the fleet. Both fabricators maintained continuity of supply through the Russian import disruption period, drawing on enrichment inventories and diversified enrichment contracts. For Constellation, the practical effect of the Russian ban and waiver regime is a managed transition over the 2024–2028 window toward Western-sourced enrichment, with contract re-tendering that carries an incremental cost increase relative to the historical Russian price points. The company's scale — operating 21-plus reactors — gives it negotiating leverage with Western enrichers and fabricators that smaller operators cannot replicate, though it also means the absolute dollar exposure to enrichment price escalation is proportionally larger.

The geopolitical overlay on the fuel cycle connects directly to the broader policy environment in which Constellation operates: the IRA Section 45U production tax credit, the federal loan support for Crane, the Trump administration's explicit framing of nuclear expansion as a national security and AI competitiveness priority, and the NRC re-licensing infrastructure that underpins the restart timeline. Dominguez, speaking to Semafor in April 2026, warned that the US was not on track to "win" the race against China's AI energy build-out without more aggressive domestic energy deployment — a political argument that aligned Constellation's commercial interests with the national-interest framing that had unlocked federal support at each stage of the Crane project.

---

*Sources: [Constellation Energy IR — Microsoft PPA announcement, September 20 2024](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-and-microsoft-reach-agreement-restore-iconic-three); [Constellation Energy IR — Meta PPA announcement, June 3 2025](https://investors.constellationenergy.com/news-releases/news-release-details/constellation-meta-sign-20-year-deal-clean-reliable-nuclear); [Utility Dive — DOE $1B loan, Crane restart](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/doe-loan-constellation-crane-nuclear-restart/805923/); [Utility Dive — PJM capacity prices record, 2024/25](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-interconnection-capacity-auction-data-center/808264/); [Utility Dive — PJM 2026/27 record $329/MW-day](https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-interconnection-capacity-auction-prices/753798/); [Constellation Energy 8-K, PJM 2027/28 auction](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001868275/000186827525000112/ceg-20251217.htm); [DOE — Russian Uranium Ban](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/russian-uranium-ban-will-speed-development-us-nuclear-fuel-supply-chain); [Congress.gov — Prohibiting Russian Uranium Imports Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/118th-congress/house-bill/1042/all-info); [Semafor — Dominguez on China AI race, April 2026](https://www.semafor.com/article/04/14/2026/constellation-energy-ceo-joe-dominguez-says-us-not-going-to-win-the-race-with-china-ai-energy-buildout)*

chapters.title: Where Constellation sits against Vistra, NRG, NextEra, and the IPP set
chapters.body:
## Scale Without Parallel

When Constellation Energy closed its acquisition of Calpine Corporation in early 2026, it created something that had not previously existed in the American power sector: a single merchant generation company operating at a scale that dwarfed every competitive peer while simultaneously holding the largest portfolio of zero-carbon baseload generation anywhere in the country. The combined entity brought together Constellation's approximately 22 gigawatts of nuclear capacity — already the largest single nuclear fleet in the United States — with Calpine's roughly 27 gigawatts of principally gas-fired and geothermal generation, producing a pro-forma fleet of approximately 49 gigawatts in competitive markets. No other independent power producer came close.

That statistical supremacy, however, did not emerge from a vacuum. It was the product of deliberate sequential moves — the IRA Section 45U production tax credit that revalued the existing nuclear fleet, the September 2024 Microsoft power purchase agreement at the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1, and then the transformative Calpine deal — that placed Constellation in a fundamentally different competitive category from its peers. Understanding where the company sits requires mapping the full terrain of the US merchant generation and utility landscape, and then interrogating whether the structural advantages are durable.

## The Merchant IPP Peer Group

The US competitive generation sector had, by the mid-2020s, consolidated around a handful of significant players following years of post-deregulation restructuring, several rounds of bankruptcy, and the more recent wave of AI-driven demand repricing.

| Company | Capacity (approx.) | Nuclear Exposure | Primary RTO Footprint | Public Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Constellation (post-Calpine) | ~49 GW | ~22 GW | PJM, MISO, NYISO, CAISO, ERCOT | NASDAQ: CEG |
| Vistra Energy | ~41 GW | ~6 GW | ERCOT, PJM | NYSE: VST |
| NRG Energy | ~18 GW | Minimal | ERCOT, PJM, broader US | NYSE: NRG |
| Talen Energy | ~13 GW | ~2.5 GW | PJM | NASDAQ: TLN |
| Calpine (pre-acquisition) | ~27 GW | None | CAISO, ERCOT, PJM | Private |

Vistra Energy was, prior to the Calpine transaction, the most direct comparable to Constellation among publicly traded merchant generators. The Dallas-based company operated approximately 41 gigawatts of generation across nuclear, natural gas, coal, solar, and battery storage assets, with its largest footprint in ERCOT — the Texas grid — supplemented by substantial PJM presence. Vistra's September 2023 acquisition of Energy Harbor added meaningful nuclear capacity: the Davis-Besse, Perry, and Beaver Valley plants contributed approximately six gigawatts of nuclear generation, giving Vistra a credible nuclear story to carry into hyperscaler PPA conversations. Vistra's ERCOT positioning also provided unique exposure to the Texas data centre buildout, where load growth from technology companies was straining the grid by 2024 and 2025. Yet Vistra's nuclear footprint — roughly six gigawatts against Constellation's 22 — remained structurally smaller, limiting the company's addressable capacity for long-duration zero-carbon contracted supply.

NRG Energy occupied a different competitive register. NRG's business model had shifted substantially toward competitive retail supply — the acquisition of Vivint Smart Home and the broader consumer and business services push — with generation increasingly serving a supporting role. NRG's nuclear exposure was minimal by comparison; the company was more comparable to a large retail electricity provider with generation assets than a nuclear-anchored merchant. The ERCOT and broader US footprint gave NRG scale in competitive retail, but it was not competing for hyperscaler nuclear PPAs in the same way as Constellation or Vistra.

Talen Energy, the smallest of the publicly traded merchant peer group, had nonetheless established a precedent of outsized competitive significance. The March 2024 announcement that Talen's Susquehanna nuclear facility in Pennsylvania had entered a data centre co-location agreement with Cumulus Data — subsequently acquired by Amazon — established the template for direct hyperscaler-to-nuclear-plant power delivery that Constellation would execute at scale seven months later. The Susquehanna-Cumulus-Amazon transaction demonstrated that a hyperscaler would pay a premium for firm zero-carbon nuclear electrons delivered directly at the plant fence, bypassing the transmission grid. When FERC subsequently intervened on co-location interconnection rules, the regulatory precedent mattered for Talen and Constellation alike. Talen's scale, however, constrained the broader opportunity; at approximately 13 gigawatts total capacity with a single large nuclear station, Talen could not offer the multi-plant, multi-region contracted supply that Constellation's 12-plant fleet enabled.

## The Nuclear-Fleet Structural Moat

The structural competitive advantage Constellation held over every peer rested on one fact: nuclear baseload generation at 22 gigawatts of scale could not be replicated. New nuclear construction in the United States carried capital costs and construction timelines that made near-term additions economically marginal in competitive markets. The nuclear fleet that Constellation inherited from Exelon was itself the product of decades of capital investment, regulatory licensing, and operational workforce development that constituted a durable barrier to entry.

That barrier had a specific financial dimension in the post-IRA framework. The Section 45U production tax credit, applicable to qualifying existing nuclear generation in tax years 2024 through 2032, provided up to approximately $15 per megawatt-hour at low power-market prices, phasing out as wholesale prices rose above roughly $25 per megawatt-hour on a gross-receipts basis. Every existing nuclear operator — Vistra after Energy Harbor, Talen at Susquehanna, Energy Harbor prior to acquisition — benefited from the 45U mechanism. But the scale of Constellation's nuclear exposure made it the single largest 45U beneficiary in the country by a substantial margin. Across approximately 22 gigawatts operating at a fleet capacity factor consistently above 90 percent, the aggregate megawatt-hour volumes subject to the 45U framework were structurally larger than any competitor's.

The effect was to install a revenue floor beneath Constellation's core earnings at a scale that no peer could match. At depressed power prices — a scenario more likely in periods of oversupply than in the AI demand surge environment of 2024 and 2025 — Constellation's nuclear fleet could capture the 45U credit to maintain effective revenue above the floor threshold. This asymmetric downside protection, combined with the upside participation in elevated power prices, fundamentally altered the risk-return profile of the nuclear fleet relative to the pre-IRA merchant model.

## Regulated Utilities and the Adjacent Landscape

Placing Constellation within the broader US electric utility sector required distinguishing between merchant IPPs and regulated utilities — a distinction that drove materially different valuation frameworks and competitive dynamics.

NextEra Energy, the largest US regulated utility by market capitalisation, was not a direct Constellation competitor but provided the most relevant scaled context. NextEra operated Florida Power & Light as a vertically integrated regulated utility alongside NextEra Energy Resources, the largest US renewables developer with wind and solar assets across 40 states. NextEra's nuclear exposure ran to approximately 5.5 gigawatts across its regulated and merchant portfolios, placing it broadly comparable to Vistra post-Energy Harbor. NextEra's competitive renewables development platform — principally wind, solar, and storage — was the largest in the country, but firm zero-carbon baseload nuclear capacity was not NextEra's differentiating asset in the hyperscaler PPA conversation in the way it was for Constellation.

Duke Energy, Southern Company, and Dominion Energy operated within vertically integrated regulated utility frameworks where generation returns were set through state rate cases and not exposed to merchant power-price volatility. These companies held substantial nuclear generation portfolios — Duke's fleet across the Carolinas, Southern's Plant Vogtle units in Georgia, Dominion's positions in Virginia and Connecticut — but the regulated cost-of-service recovery model meant their nuclear assets were not available for merchant hyperscaler PPA contracting in the same manner. Duke and Southern were building new nuclear through the AP1000 programme; Southern's Unit 3 at Vogtle reached commercial operation in mid-2023, Unit 4 in late 2023, representing the first new US nuclear construction completion in over three decades. But those assets remained inside regulated rate base rather than merchant markets.

Pure-play renewables developers — NextEra Energy Resources, AES Corporation, Brookfield Renewable — occupied a category defined by intermittency. Wind and solar generation, while cost-competitive on a levelised basis, could not provide the 24-hour, 365-day firm carbon-free power that hyperscalers specified in their data centre supply requirements. AES and Brookfield could contract renewable megawatts at scale, but the product lacked the firm dispatchable characteristics that nuclear generation uniquely provided. This technical distinction drove the premium pricing embedded in Constellation's hyperscaler PPA economics relative to comparable renewable power purchase agreements.

## PJM Positioning and the Capacity Market Uplift

Constellation's geographic concentration in PJM — the largest US grid operator covering 13 mid-Atlantic and Midwest states plus the District of Columbia — provided a specific capacity market advantage that diverged from Vistra's ERCOT-weighted profile. PJM's capacity market, which procured forward reserves through periodic Base Residual Auctions, cleared the 2025-2026 delivery year at prices above $269 per megawatt-day across most of the territory — a level reflecting the first wave of AI data centre load additions and sharply tightened reserve margins. Constrained zones, notably in the Chicago metropolitan area and parts of the Midwest where Constellation's Illinois nuclear fleet was concentrated, cleared at higher prices still.

For Constellation's PJM-located nuclear fleet — Byron, Braidwood, Dresden, Quad Cities, Clinton, and LaSalle in Illinois; Peach Bottom and Limerick in Pennsylvania; Calvert Cliffs in Maryland — the elevated capacity prices represented a substantial incremental revenue layer above energy market economics. Vistra captured capacity revenue in PJM and ERCOT, but ERCOT's capacity market structure differed materially from PJM's administratively determined capacity product, and the 2024-2025 PJM auction outcomes specifically rewarded Constellation's PJM nuclear positioning.

## Hyperscaler PPA Execution as the Differentiating Variable

If nuclear-fleet scale and Section 45U exposure defined the structural competitive position, the differentiating execution variable was the pace and terms of hyperscaler PPA contracting. Talen's March 2024 Susquehanna-Amazon co-location deal established the proof of concept. Constellation's September 2024 Microsoft agreement at the restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1 established the template at scale — a 20-year, 835-megawatt agreement that committed Microsoft to the full output of the Crane Clean Energy Center restart, with Constellation investing approximately $1.6 billion in the plant refurbishment and NRC re-licensing process.

The Microsoft deal's significance extended beyond its economics. It demonstrated that a hyperscaler would enter a 20-year offtake commitment for nuclear generation at a premium sufficient to justify a multi-billion dollar restart investment in a plant that had been shuttered since 2019. It also demonstrated that Constellation, operating 12 nuclear plants rather than Talen's one, could sequence additional hyperscaler transactions across its portfolio — a pipeline optionality that no peer possessed at equivalent scale.

Vistra engaged in its own hyperscaler conversations through 2024 and 2025, and the company's nuclear plants in PJM were credible assets for similar transactions. But six gigawatts of nuclear capacity across three plants in one RTO offered a materially smaller addressable pipeline than Constellation's 22 gigawatts across 12 plants in PJM, MISO, and NYISO.

## The Post-Calpine Strategic Position

The January 2025 Calpine acquisition resolved the one structural gap in Constellation's competitive positioning: dispatchable capacity. Nuclear generation, operating as must-run baseload, could not ramp to meet short-duration demand spikes or serve peaking requirements. Calpine's approximately 27 gigawatts of principally gas-fired combined-cycle and peaking generation, concentrated in CAISO, ERCOT, and PJM, provided the flexible capacity complement. The Geysers geothermal portfolio added approximately 725 megawatts of firm renewable generation in California. Together, the combined entity could offer a hyperscaler or large industrial customer a bundled solution — nuclear baseload plus gas-fired dispatchable backup plus renewable certificates — across multiple grid regions.

The pro-forma entity's scale surpassed Vistra's approximately 41 gigawatts and established a new category in US merchant generation. The competitive question going forward was whether that scale advantage translated into durable return advantages, or whether the gas-fired generation assets — price-exposed to natural gas commodity cycles and facing longer-term policy risk — diluted the nuclear pure-play thesis that had driven the equity's re-rating. The answer depended on three variables: the pace of hyperscaler PPA contracting across the nuclear fleet, the durability of the Section 45U PTC framework through 2032 and any extensions beyond, and the trajectory of the broader merchant power cycle across PJM, ERCOT, and CAISO.

chapters.title: From the 2022 spin through TMI to the Calpine close
chapters.body:
## A clean break, a new market

Constellation Energy Corporation began trading on the NASDAQ on the morning of February 1, 2022, completing a corporate separation from Exelon that had been announced the prior July. The split cleaved the old Exelon vertically: the six regulated distribution utilities — ComEd, PECO, BGE, ACE, Pepco, Delmarva — stayed with the Exelon parent, while the merchant generation fleet and competitive supply business became the standalone company under the ticker CEG. What Constellation inherited was simultaneously the largest nuclear fleet in the United States and a business model that had spent the prior decade fighting for its economic survival in wholesale power markets depressed by cheap natural gas and subsidised renewables.

Joe Dominguez, elevated from his role running Exelon's Illinois and Pennsylvania utilities to become the first CEO of the reconstituted standalone, framed the spin as a strategic unlock rather than a distress disposal. The thesis was straightforward: the merchant fleet, freed from cross-subsidy obligations to regulated utility siblings, could be managed expressly for clean-energy commercial value. At spin, the company reported approximately 22 gigawatts of nuclear capacity across twelve plants, producing roughly 10 percent of the clean electricity generated in the United States. The adjusted EBITDA in 2022 reached approximately $2.7 billion against revenues of approximately $24.4 billion — a margin structure reflecting both the nuclear fleet's near-zero fuel cost and the residual volatility of merchant power pricing.

The equity opened to cautious reception. Merchant nuclear operators carried an institutional stigma earned across a decade of impairments and plant closures. The critical policy variable — whether Congress would intervene to support existing nuclear economics through the tax code — remained unresolved at the time of the February spin.

## The IRA floor

That question was answered six months later. The Inflation Reduction Act, enacted in August 2022, introduced Section 45U of the Internal Revenue Code — a production tax credit of up to approximately $15 per megawatt-hour for zero-emission electricity generated at existing nuclear facilities, applicable for tax years 2024 through 2032. The credit is structured with a phase-out mechanism above a gross-receipts threshold of approximately $25 per MWh, meaning the effective benefit is highest in low-power-price environments and tapers as realised prices rise. For investors, the practical significance was transformative: the 45U PTC converted what had been a pure commodity play — nuclear generation whose economics lived and died with forward power curves — into a structure with a meaningful revenue floor.

Constellation's nuclear fleet qualified for the credit at essentially its full generating capacity. At a blended 45U value, the fleet benefit amounted to hundreds of millions of dollars annually in avoided downside, concentrated precisely in the years when low power prices would previously have eroded earnings most severely. Daniel Eggers, the CFO who had joined Constellation in December 2021 just ahead of the spin, described the 45U structure in subsequent earnings communications as a material improvement to the company's risk-adjusted earnings profile — the floor mechanism that reframed what had been a binary commodity bet as a structured income stream with upside participation.

The EBITDA trajectory validates the sequence: $2.7 billion in 2022 (pre-45U), $3.8 billion in 2023 (the year of enactment and anticipation), $4.8 billion in 2024 (first full 45U qualifying year combined with rising power prices and the AI demand pull beginning to affect forward curves). The near-doubling of EBITDA across three years of post-spin operation reflected both the policy tailwind and an emerging commercial development that by late 2024 would reframe the investment thesis entirely.

## Three Mile Island: from closure to template

The backstory to what became Constellation's most consequential transaction in the first four years of its public life was a shutdown decision made five years before the company existed in its current form. In September 2019, Exelon announced the permanent closure of Three Mile Island Unit 1 — the 835-megawatt pressurised water reactor in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, that had operated since 1974 and whose name carried the permanent resonance of the 1979 Unit 2 accident. The economics were straightforward and brutal: low wholesale power prices in PJM, absent a state zero-emission credit programme comparable to those in Illinois or New York, made continued operation untenable. Unit 1 shut down on September 20, 2019.

The closure passed into the merchant nuclear narrative as another data point on the fragility of unsubsidised baseload economics. What changed over the following five years — the IRA 45U PTC, the emergence of AI data centre operators as large-scale purchasers of guaranteed clean electricity, and the growing recognition that the US grid had far too little firm dispatchable capacity to absorb the coming demand surge — meant that the political and commercial logic that had forced the shutdown was, by 2024, running in reverse.

## The September 2024 inflection

On September 20, 2024, Constellation and Microsoft announced a twenty-year power purchase agreement under which Microsoft would purchase the full output of a restarted Three Mile Island Unit 1. The plant was to be renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, honouring Christopher Crane, the former Exelon CEO who had managed the nuclear fleet through its most difficult decade and who died in April 2022 shortly after the spin. Constellation committed approximately $1.6 billion to the restart project — covering refurbishment of the shuttered plant, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission re-licensing process, and the physical infrastructure needed to bring an 835-megawatt reactor back to commercial operation after a five-year cold shutdown. Target restart was 2028.

The transaction represented the first time a hyperscale technology company had contracted for the full output of a restarting US nuclear plant under a long-duration PPA. Dominguez described the agreement as validation of nuclear energy's unique fitness for the AI infrastructure buildout — a reliable, carbon-free baseload supply that renewable intermittency could not replicate at the scale and reliability requirements that frontier AI training clusters demanded. The press release language from that morning framed the restart explicitly as a template, with Constellation signalling that the commercial structure — long-dated PPA, full-output offtake, carbon-free attribute — was one it intended to replicate across the broader nuclear fleet as additional hyperscaler conversations matured.

The equity market response was pronounced. Shares in CEG had already begun appreciating through 2023 and into 2024 as the AI data centre electricity demand thesis gathered consensus and the 45U PTC began flowing. The September 2024 announcement crystallised the monetisation model: Constellation was not merely a passive beneficiary of rising wholesale power prices but an active counterparty capable of structuring decade-spanning bilateral contracts with the most creditworthy corporate buyers in the world. The hyperscaler PPA became the principal valuation narrative for the stock.

## Capacity market confirmation

The commercial logic of the September 2024 announcement was reinforced by developments in the PJM Interconnection capacity market. The 2025-2026 capacity auction, conducted in July 2024, cleared at substantially elevated prices — above $269 per megawatt-day across most of the PJM footprint, with constrained zones settling higher still. The auction result reflected the simultaneous pressure of accelerating AI data centre load growth, the retirement of older thermal generation, and the long interconnection queues that prevented new supply from entering service quickly enough to offset the demand increase. Constellation's PJM nuclear fleet — Byron, Braidwood, Calvert Cliffs, Clinton, Dresden, Limerick, Peach Bottom, Quad Cities, and the restarting Crane Clean Energy Center — captured capacity revenue at these elevated clearing prices across essentially the full nuclear megawatt-hour base in the region.

## The Calpine acquisition

The scale of ambition became clearer on January 10, 2025, when Constellation announced an agreement to acquire Calpine Corporation for approximately $26.6 billion in total consideration. The structure combined approximately $16.4 billion in cash, approximately 50 million CEG shares valued at approximately $10.2 billion at announcement, and the assumption of approximately $12.7 billion in Calpine net debt. Calpine — owned by a consortium including Energy Capital Partners, Access Industries, and the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board — was the largest privately-held power producer in the United States, operating approximately 27 gigawatts of generation principally through natural-gas-fired combined-cycle plants supplemented by The Geysers geothermal complex in Northern California, the largest geothermal facility in North America.

The strategic rationale operated on multiple dimensions. Dispatchable gas-fired capacity would complement the nuclear baseload in the bundled offtake structures that hyperscaler customers increasingly required — not carbon-free for every megawatt-hour, but reliability guarantees that firm gas generation could provide when nuclear was in scheduled refuelling outages. Geographic diversification extended Constellation into ERCOT in Texas and CAISO in California, markets where the company had previously had minimal operating presence. The geothermal portfolio added a category of firm renewable generation — baseload dispatchable clean energy — that commanded a premium from corporate offtakers pursuing scope-two emissions targets. Closing was targeted for late 2025 or early 2026, subject to Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, NRC, and other regulatory approvals alongside Calpine shareholder consent. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the regulatory review process remained the governing gating item on the timeline.

## Forward catalysts

From the snapshot date, the principal near-term catalysts for the equity thesis fell into three clusters. The Calpine integration — however the close timing resolved across the late-2025-to-early-2026 window — represented the most immediate earnings-per-share event, adding substantial gas and geothermal generation EBITDA and creating a scaled US merchant generation platform without precedent in market capitalisation or generating diversity. The Crane Clean Energy Center restart programme, with its 2028 target commercial operation date, remained on the critical path for the Microsoft PPA revenue to begin flowing and for the restart template to be empirically proven at scale. And the broader hyperscaler PPA pipeline — which Constellation's earnings communications through 2024 and into 2025 described as active and expanded — represented the next leg of the commercial valuation story, with additional long-duration bilateral offtake agreements potentially announced against the balance of the nuclear fleet or against capacity additions at existing licensed sites.

NRC re-licensing milestones at individual plants — Dresden, Quad Cities, and several others with licences approaching extension deadlines — carried their own catalytic weight, each successful extension extending the earnings duration of the relevant generating asset by twenty years.

## Specialist commentary

*Specialist commentary framing of CEG by Aleabit was not surfaced in the bounded primary-source set.*

Among the narrower analyst and independent commentary community engaged with the nuclear-AI intersection through 2024 and into 2025, the dominant framing treated the September 2024 Microsoft transaction as the event that validated what had previously been a theoretical proposition — that hyperscale technology operators would pay a structurally higher price for guaranteed carbon-free baseload than the wholesale market would clear, creating a bilateral power market running above the ISO marginal-cost price. The implication for the remaining uncontracted nuclear fleet was straightforward: every megawatt-hour of nuclear output that could be structured into a long-dated hyperscaler PPA above wholesale clearing prices represented incremental equity value relative to the pre-2024 merchant valuation model.

| Nuclear fleet capacity (GW) | ~22 | ~22 | ~22 |
